title: “BY THEIR FRUIT YOU WILL KNOW THEM” — JESUS SAID FRUIT, NOT GIFTS
paragraphs: “BY THEIR FRUIT YOU WILL KNOW THEM” — JESUS SAID FRUIT, NOT GIFTS
The Most Dangerous Spiritual Deception Is Not Always Found in Someone Who Denies Jesus. Sometimes It Is Found in Someone Who Speaks His Name Beautifully but Refuses to Live Under His Lordship.
What if the person who taught you how to pray was secretly destroying someone else's faith?
What if the voice that moved you to tears during worship belonged to someone who went home and treated their family with cruelty?
What if the person who could quote entire chapters of Scripture could not bring themselves to say three simple words?
“I was wrong.”
And here is the question that should make every one of us uncomfortable.
What if that person is not somebody else?
What if it is you?
What if it is me?
Because somewhere between the applause of a congregation and the silence of a locked bedroom, there is a truth we desperately need to confront.
A person can know the language of Christianity without displaying the character of Christ.
A person can be admired publicly and remain spiritually unhealthy privately.
A person can have extraordinary gifts and still desperately need repentance.
And perhaps the most frightening possibility is that we can become so fascinated with what God allows someone to do that we stop examining who that person is becoming.
Jesus knew this danger long before Christianity had microphones, television ministries, viral sermons, or millions of followers.
He warned us about it in words so simple that even a child could remember them.
And so piercing that even the most celebrated religious leader should tremble before them.
“Wherefore by their fruits ye shall know them.” — Matthew 7:20, KJV
Not by their popularity.
Not by their eloquence.
Not by the number of people who admire them.
Not even by the extraordinary things they claim to have accomplished in His name.
By their fruits.
But before we turn those words into another weapon against people who have disappointed us, we need to understand something.
Jesus did not give us this warning merely so we could examine everyone else.
He gave it so that truth could expose deception, including the deception hiding inside our own hearts.
And what He said immediately afterward may be one of the most sobering warnings in the entire New Testament.
Imagine standing in a crowded church.
The worship is powerful. Hands are lifted. Tears are falling. The preacher speaks with extraordinary confidence.
People testify that lives have changed through the ministry.
Everything appears blessed.
Then imagine that the service ends.
The music stops.
The congregation leaves.
The preacher walks into a private room, and the person who seemed so gentle behind the pulpit becomes someone entirely different.
The kindness disappears.
The humility evaporates.
The words become sharp.
The people closest to that person know a version of them that the congregation has never seen.
This is not an accusation against every gifted minister. Many faithful servants of Christ demonstrate genuine humility, integrity, and love both publicly and privately.
But the possibility of a divided life is precisely why Jesus told His followers to exercise discernment.
In Matthew 7:15, He warned:
“Beware of false prophets, which come to you in sheep's clothing, but inwardly they are ravening wolves.”
Notice the imagery.
The danger does not always announce itself with obvious wickedness.
Sometimes it comes dressed in familiarity.
Sometimes it knows the right words.
Sometimes it looks exactly like what we expected a spiritual leader to look like.
And that is why Jesus directs our attention away from appearance and toward fruit.
The original Greek of Matthew 7:20 reads:
ἄρα γε ἀπὸ τῶν καρπῶν αὐτῶν ἐπιγνώσεσθε αὐτούς.
Ara ge apo tōn karpōn autōn epignōsesthe autous.
A close translation is:
“So then, from their fruits you will recognize them.”
The word καρπῶν (karpōn) means “fruits,” the plural form of karpos, a word used for literal fruit and, figuratively, for the results or products of a life.
The verb ἐπιγνώσεσθε (epignōsesthe) means “you will recognize” or “you will know.”
Jesus is describing discernment based on what a life produces.
Not merely what a person claims.
Not merely what others say about them.
Not merely what appears impressive from a distance.
He uses an illustration that is almost impossible to misunderstand.
A good tree produces good fruit.
A bad tree produces bad fruit.
The nature of the tree is revealed through what grows from it.
And here is where the warning becomes painfully personal.
A microphone can amplify a voice, but it cannot manufacture holiness.
A title can establish a position, but it cannot create integrity.
A spiritual gift can benefit others, but it is not, by itself, proof of spiritual maturity.
This distinction matters because the Bible never teaches that spiritual gifts are evil or unimportant.
They are gifts of grace.
Paul writes in 1 Corinthians 12:7:
Spiritual gifts are given for the common good.
Teaching matters.
Prophecy must be tested.
Service matters.
Encouragement matters.
God's people are called to steward what He has entrusted to them.
But gifts and fruit are not interchangeable.
A gift concerns what God graciously enables a person to contribute.
Spiritual fruit concerns the character produced through the Holy Spirit's work in a life that belongs to Christ.
And Scripture gives us a devastating example of what happens when giftedness is mistaken for godliness.
The church in Corinth was not lacking in spiritual gifts.
Paul acknowledged this in 1 Corinthians 1:7.
Yet the same congregation struggled with jealousy, divisions, pride, sexual immorality, disorder, and a failure to love one another.
They had spiritual gifts.
But their conduct exposed serious spiritual immaturity.
And when Paul addressed the problem, he did not tell them to pursue more impressive performances as the solution.
He placed love at the center.
In 1 Corinthians 13:1, he wrote:
“Though I speak with the tongues of men and of angels, and have not charity, I am become as sounding brass, or a tinkling cymbal.”
The Greek word translated “charity” in the King James Version is ἀγάπη (agapē), meaning love.
Not merely emotional affection.
Not religious excitement.
But the kind of love Paul describes as patient, kind, not boastful, not arrogant, not self-seeking, and unwilling to rejoice in wrongdoing.
Then he goes further.
In 1 Corinthians 13:2, Paul explains that even extraordinary spiritual knowledge, prophetic ability, and faith capable of moving mountains leave him as nothing if he lacks love.
Think about that.
A person could astonish a crowd and still fail the test of love.
Someone could speak about God's mercy and refuse to extend mercy.
Someone could teach forgiveness and nourish bitterness.
Someone could preach repentance and become furious whenever confronted about their own sin.
And suddenly the question is no longer, “How gifted are they?”
It becomes:
“Where is the love of Christ in the way they live?”
This is not a call to despise gifts.
It is a call to stop using gifts as an excuse to ignore character.
Because the Bible does not present spiritual ability as a substitute for obedience.
And Jesus makes that terrifyingly clear only a few verses after His warning about fruit.
In Matthew 7:22–23, He says:
“Many will say to me in that day, Lord, Lord, have we not prophesied in thy name? and in thy name have cast out devils? and in thy name done many wonderful works?
And then will I profess unto them, I never knew you: depart from me, ye that work iniquity.”
Read that again.
Slowly.
These are not people claiming they openly rejected Jesus.
They are people appealing to religious activity performed in His name.
They point to prophecy.
They point to deliverance.
They point to mighty works.
But Jesus points to something they cannot overcome with a religious résumé.
“I never knew you.”
The Greek text of Matthew 7:23 includes these words:
οὐδέποτε ἔγνων ὑμᾶς
Oudepote egnōn hymas.
“I never knew you.”
And the warning concludes:
οἱ ἐργαζόμενοι τὴν ἀνομίαν
Hoi ergazomenoi tēn anomian.
“You who practice lawlessness.”
The word ἀνομία (anomia) refers to lawlessness, a disregard for what is right before God.
Jesus is not teaching that believers earn salvation by producing an impressive record of moral achievements.
He is exposing the danger of claiming allegiance to Him while remaining committed to lawlessness.
That distinction is everything.
Because salvation is not purchased through good behavior.
Ephesians 2:8–9 declares that we are saved by grace through faith, not by works.
But the very next verse tells us that believers are created in Christ Jesus for good works.
Grace does not mean that transformation is unnecessary.
Grace is the very reason transformation becomes possible.
We are not saved because we bear fruit. We bear fruit because God's saving grace is at work in us.
And when genuine faith takes root, it does not remain permanently indifferent to the character of the Savior.
This brings us to the passage that reveals what spiritual fruit actually looks like.
Galatians 5:22–23:
“But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, longsuffering, gentleness, goodness, faith,
Meekness, temperance: against such there is no law.”
The Greek begins:
Ὁ δὲ καρπὸς τοῦ πνεύματός ἐστιν ἀγάπη
Ho de karpos tou pneumatos estin agapē.
“But the fruit of the Spirit is love...”
Notice something beautiful.
Paul uses the singular καρπός (karpos) — fruit.
He describes the Spirit's fruit through a connected series of qualities that reflect the Spirit's transforming work.
Love.
Joy.
Peace.
Patience.
Kindness.
Goodness.
Faithfulness.
Gentleness.
Self-control.
The King James Version uses “longsuffering,” “faith,” and “temperance,” where many modern translations use “patience,” “faithfulness,” and “self-control.”
These are not competing messages. They are translation choices that help express the meaning of the Greek terms in context.
And none of these qualities requires a stage.
You do not need a microphone to be patient.
You do not need a congregation to be gentle.
You do not need a ministry title to practice self-control.
You do not need an audience to tell the truth.
You do not need applause to forgive someone.
In fact, some of the clearest evidence of spiritual growth appears in places where nobody is watching.
When you are exhausted and still choose not to humiliate your spouse.
When your child makes a mistake and you correct them without cruelty.
When you have the opportunity to retaliate and instead entrust justice to God.
When you admit that your words wounded someone.
When you refuse to exploit the vulnerability of a person who trusts you.
When you turn away from a temptation that nobody else would have discovered.
When you stop defending a sin simply because admitting it would cost you your reputation.
These moments may never become testimonies shared before thousands.
But they matter to God.
And perhaps someone reading this knows the pain of discovering that the person who taught them about God's love did not practice that love at home.
Perhaps you were raised in a house where Scripture was quoted loudly but apologies were almost never spoken.
Perhaps your father prayed publicly but frightened everyone privately.
Perhaps your mother served faithfully at church while your deepest emotional wounds remained unacknowledged.
Perhaps a spiritual leader demanded loyalty while refusing accountability.
Perhaps you were told that questioning harmful behavior meant you were rebelling against God.
And perhaps, after everything you experienced, you began wondering whether Christianity itself was the problem.
Please hear this carefully.
The hypocrisy of someone who speaks for Jesus does not erase the truth of Jesus.
Christ never commanded you to call cruelty holiness.
He never taught that spiritual authority gives someone permission to abuse others.
He never told His followers to confuse religious performance with genuine righteousness.
Jesus confronted religious hypocrisy directly.
In Matthew 23, He condemned leaders who emphasized outward religious appearance while neglecting justice, mercy, and faithfulness.
He did not defend their hypocrisy because they possessed religious status.
He exposed it.
And if you have been wounded by someone who used the name of Jesus while behaving in ways contrary to His teaching, your pain should not be dismissed.
You are not required to pretend the harm was harmless.
Forgiveness does not mean denying the truth.
Reconciliation does not mean abandoning wisdom or safety.
And spiritual discernment does not require surrendering your conscience to someone simply because they possess a title.
Jesus remains worthy of your trust even when someone who claimed to represent Him has betrayed it.
But there is another side to this message.
And it may be harder to hear.
Because it is possible to spend so much time identifying bad fruit in others that we forget to examine the fruit growing in our own lives.
It is easy to criticize an arrogant preacher.
But what happens when someone corrects us?
It is easy to condemn a dishonest leader.
But are we honest when telling the truth costs us something?
It is easy to expose someone else's hypocrisy.
But what happens when our private behavior contradicts our public testimony?
We can share Christian content every day and still refuse to forgive.
We can post Bible verses and still entertain cruelty in our conversations.
We can defend sound doctrine online and still neglect compassion toward the people living under our roof.
We can speak passionately about holiness while secretly protecting habits we know dishonor God.
And the uncomfortable truth is this:
A person can be right in an argument and still be wrong in spirit.
That does not mean truth should be sacrificed for politeness.
Jesus Himself spoke difficult truths.
It means that the truth we defend should increasingly shape the character with which we defend it.
So before we use Matthew 7 to examine every preacher, teacher, worship leader, or Christian influencer, perhaps we should sit quietly with God and ask:
“Lord, what is growing in me?”
Not, “How many people agree with me?”
Not, “How many people shared my testimony?”
Not, “How many people admire my faith?”
But:
“Am I becoming more loving?”
“Am I becoming more truthful?”
“Am I more willing to repent?”
“Am I gentler with those who cannot offer me anything?”
“Am I learning to obey You when obedience is costly?”
And if those questions expose something painful, do not run from the light.
Run toward Jesus.
Because the purpose of conviction is not to leave a repentant sinner hopeless.
It is to bring what is hidden into the presence of the Savior who forgives and transforms.

There is a difference between a struggling believer who hates their sin and keeps returning to Christ in repentance, and a person who deliberately protects wrongdoing while demanding spiritual admiration.
There is a difference between immaturity and calculated deception.
There is a difference between falling into sin and making peace with it.
Christians are not sinless people.
Even sincere believers struggle, fail, and require ongoing correction.
First John 1:8 warns that claiming to have no sin is self-deception.
And 1 John 1:9 offers this promise:
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.”
This is why spiritual fruit must never become a tool for demanding instant perfection from ourselves or others.
Fruit grows.
It develops over time.
It is nourished.
It can be hindered by neglect.
And it is recognized through the ongoing direction and pattern of a life, not by a single impressive moment or one isolated failure.
A young believer may still struggle with impatience.
A mature believer may experience a season of profound grief.
A faithful Christian may be exhausted, wounded, or battling temptation.
None of these experiences automatically proves the absence of the Holy Spirit.
But when the Spirit is at work, He leads us toward repentance, truth, love, and obedience rather than teaching us to celebrate or conceal sin.
And this is where the Gospel becomes breathtaking.
Because Jesus did not merely command His followers to produce fruit and then leave them alone to accomplish the impossible.
He told them where the life required for fruitfulness comes from.
In John 15:5, Jesus declares:
“I am the vine, ye are the branches: He that abideth in me, and I in him, the same bringeth forth much fruit: for without me ye can do nothing.”
In the Greek, Jesus says:
ἐγώ εἰμι ἡ ἄμπελος, ὑμεῖς τὰ κλήματα
Egō eimi hē ampelos, hymeis ta klēmata.
“I am the vine; you are the branches.”
Then comes the essential truth:
χωρὶς ἐμοῦ οὐ δύνασθε ποιεῖν οὐδέν
Chōris emou ou dynasthe poiein ouden.
“Apart from me you can do nothing.”
There it is.
The secret is not trying to look more fruitful than the person beside you.
The secret is abiding in Christ.
Remaining dependent on Him.
Receiving His Word.
Walking in His truth.
Turning from sin.
Seeking His help.
Allowing His Spirit to transform what human willpower alone cannot heal.
A branch does not produce grapes by painting grapes onto itself.
It bears fruit because it remains connected to the vine.
And this is the tragedy of performance-driven Christianity.
We can become so busy trying to appear spiritually impressive that we neglect the very relationship through which spiritual transformation takes place.
We learn how to sound holy before we learn how to surrender.
We learn how to build a platform before we learn how to carry a cross.
We learn how to impress Christians before we learn how to love people.
And sometimes God, in His mercy, allows our carefully constructed image to crack.
Not because He delights in humiliating us.
But because what is hidden must sometimes be confronted before genuine healing can begin.
Consider Peter.
He was bold.
Passionate.
Certain of his devotion.
He declared that even if others fell away, he would remain faithful.
Yet when fear overtook him, he denied knowing Jesus three times.
Imagine the shame.
The man who had spoken so confidently about loyalty could not withstand the pressure of a courtyard confrontation.
Luke 22:61–62 tells us that after Peter's denial, the Lord turned and looked at him.
Peter remembered Jesus' words.
And he went out and wept bitterly.
What did Peter have left to boast about?
Not his courage.
Not his consistency.
Not his flawless devotion.
His failure had exposed him.
But his failure was not the end of his story.
After the resurrection, Jesus restored Peter in a deeply personal encounter recorded in John 21.
Three times Jesus asked Peter about his love.
And He entrusted him with the responsibility to care for His sheep.
The man who had denied Him was not beyond the reach of His restoring grace.
Peter's restoration was not permission to treat denial casually.
It was evidence that repentance and grace can open a future that failure seemed to have destroyed.
That is the difference Jesus makes.
He does not merely improve our religious image.
He confronts the truth about us and offers redemption.
And maybe that is what someone reading this needs to hear today.
You have spent years trying to appear stronger than you really are.
You have smiled through spiritual exhaustion.
You have hidden resentment behind religious language.
You have spoken about forgiveness while carrying wounds you never brought honestly before God.
You have tried to convince everyone that you are doing well.
But privately, you know there are things that need to change.
Perhaps you are not the person who wounded others.
Perhaps you are the person who has been wounded and is struggling not to become bitter.
Perhaps you are both.
Perhaps you have harmed someone and been harmed yourself.
And now you are afraid that admitting the truth will destroy the identity you have spent years protecting.
But listen.
Jesus did not go to the cross to rescue a fictional, polished version of you.
He came to save sinners.
Real sinners.
People with regrets.
People with shame.
People who have failed.
People who cannot repair their own hearts.
Romans 5:8 declares:
“But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.”
Not after we became impressive.
Not after we built a spotless reputation.
Not after we learned how to hide every weakness.
While we were still sinners.
Christ died for us.
The sinless Son of God bore our sins on the cross.
He rose from the dead.
And through Him, forgiveness and reconciliation with God are offered to those who repent and believe.
This is the heart of the Gospel.
Not that sinners can become excellent religious performers.
But that sinners can be forgiven, reconciled to God, and transformed through Jesus Christ.
The Gospel does not merely change the ending of our story.
It changes who we are becoming.
From pride to humility.
From deception to truth.
From bitterness to forgiveness.
From spiritual performance to sincere devotion.
Not because the scandal was insignificant.
Not because wrongdoing should be excused.
Not because consequences disappear.
But because Jesus Christ is able to redeem lives that sin has devastated.
And there is one more truth we must not overlook.
In Matthew 7, Jesus tells us to recognize people by their fruit.
But He never authorizes us to pretend that we can see every secret of the human heart.
Final judgment belongs to God.
Discernment belongs to the responsibilities He has given us.
We can evaluate teaching against Scripture.
We can examine patterns of behavior.
We can refuse to excuse manipulation, exploitation, and persistent unrepentant wrongdoing.
We can protect vulnerable people.
We can seek accountability.
We can test spiritual claims.
But we must resist the temptation to appoint ourselves as infallible judges of another person's eternal destiny.
The same Jesus who warned against false prophets also warned against hypocritical judgment earlier in Matthew 7.
Biblical discernment is not gossip dressed in religious language.
It is not envy disguised as righteousness.
It is not destroying someone's reputation because we dislike their personality.
And it is certainly not treating every weakness as proof that someone is a false Christian.
True discernment requires truth, humility, patience, evidence, and obedience to God's Word.
It recognizes that fruit matters.
And it remembers that we, too, stand in need of grace.
So here is the question I want to leave in your heart.
When the applause disappears...
When nobody is watching...
When your title no longer impresses anyone...
When your social media account is silent...
When the sermon is over and the worship music fades...
Who are you becoming in the presence of Jesus?
Because one day, every platform will be silent.
Every earthly title will lose its power to impress.
Every reputation will stand beneath the perfect knowledge of God.
And the question will not be whether we successfully convinced people that we belonged to Christ.
What matters is whether we truly belong to Him.
Do we know Him?
Have we trusted Him?
Are we abiding in Him?
Is His grace changing the direction of our lives?
Do not mistake religious visibility for intimacy with God.
Do not mistake talent for holiness.
Do not mistake emotional excitement for spiritual maturity.
And do not mistake a public gift for private obedience.
If you have been trusting in your religious accomplishments instead of Christ, come back to the Gospel.
If you have been using your gifts to avoid confronting your character, repent.
If you have been wounded by hypocrisy, do not let the failures of people keep you from the Savior who condemned hypocrisy.
If you have fallen, do not remain on the ground pretending that you cannot rise.
Come to Jesus.
Confess what is true.
Receive His mercy.
Make restitution where appropriate and possible.
Accept accountability.
And walk forward in the newness of life that His grace makes possible.
Because the most beautiful testimony is not always the person who can command the attention of thousands.
Sometimes it is the father who finally apologizes to his child.
The husband who stops using Scripture to win arguments and begins practicing sacrificial love.
The wife who chooses truth over appearances.
The ministry leader who welcomes correction instead of silencing it.
The believer who breaks a destructive habit and seeks help.
The wounded soul who begins learning to trust Christ again.
The person who once loved being admired but now longs to become more like Jesus.
No spotlight.
No applause.
No extraordinary public performance.
Just grace quietly producing fruit.
And heaven is not confused about the difference.
If this message has exposed something you have been avoiding, please do not bury that conviction beneath another religious performance.
Bring it to the Lord.
You do not need to reveal private details to be honest before God.
And if you have witnessed Christ change your character, your testimony may encourage someone who believes they will never change.
There may also be someone in your life who desperately needs this message.
Not because you want to embarrass them.
Not because you want to win an argument.
But because you love them enough to point them toward Jesus.
Invite your family, friends, fellow believers, struggling Christians, and even those who are still searching for truth to follow as well.
Because the Gospel is not meant to remain trapped inside the walls of our own comfort.
It is good news worth sharing.
And if this ministry has been helping you grow in God's Word, I want to invite you into something deeper.

Not merely as someone who enjoys Christian articles, but as someone who wants to help sustain and expand the work of sharing Scripture, encouraging believers, reaching seekers, and pointing people back to Jesus Christ.
Scripture teaches in 2 Corinthians 9:7:
“Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.”
That is the spirit in which this invitation is offered.
Not guilt.
Not pressure.
Every monthly contribution helps provide ongoing support for the creation and sharing of biblical teaching, Gospel-centered articles, encouragement, and discipleship resources.
You never know whose life may be reached through one faithful act of sharing.
These resources are part of our desire to make biblical nourishment and Christian growth more accessible.
The greater invitation is to participate in something that points beyond merchandise, beyond content, and beyond any individual ministry.
A continuing mission to make Jesus Christ known.
Gospel Warrior is not the vine.
No ministry is.
No preacher is.
No Christian platform is.
Jesus Christ alone is the true Vine.
Our purpose is not to make people dependent on a ministry.
It is to continually point people toward the Savior who gives life.
Spend a moment alone with Jesus.
Ask Him to examine your heart.
Ask Him to expose what is false.
Ask Him to heal what is wounded.
Ask Him to forgive what is sinful.
Ask Him to strengthen what is weak.
And ask Him to produce in you the kind of fruit that cannot be manufactured by applause.
Because you may forget the sermon that made you cry.
You may forget the voice that gave you goosebumps.
You may forget the name of the person who impressed you most.
But you will remember the person who loved you when you were difficult to love.
The person who told the truth when lying would have been easier.
The person who apologized when pride demanded silence.
The person who showed you something of Jesus without needing to announce how spiritual they were.
And perhaps, through the grace of God, you can become that person for someone else.
Not perfect.
Not famous.
Not always strong.
But repentant.
Faithful.
Growing.
Abiding in Christ.
Bearing fruit that points beyond yourself to the Savior.
Because when Jesus said, “By their fruits ye shall know them,” He gave us more than a warning about deceptive religious leaders.
He gave us a reason to examine what our lives are revealing about the One we claim to follow.
When the world forgets the sound of your voice, may someone still remember the love of Jesus they encountered through your life.
